entries.75a20d47832e4e40bacfdf1edb78924c156802b7: <div sID="gen15317" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="6" osisID="Song.6" sID="Song.6"/> <div eID="gen15317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15318" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15319" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, I. The daughters of Jerusalem, moved with the description which the church had given of Christ, enquire after him, <reference osisRef="Song.6.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. The church directs them where they may meet with him, <reference osisRef="Song.6.2-Song.6.3">ver. 2, 3</reference>. III. Christ is now found of those that sought him, and very highly applauds the beauty of his spouse, as one extremely smitten with it (<reference osisRef="Song.6.4-Song.6.7">ver. 4-7</reference>), preferring her before all others (<reference osisRef="Song.6.8-Song.6.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>), recommending her to the love and esteem of all her neighbours (<reference osisRef="Song.6.10">ver. 10</reference>), and, lastly, acknowledging the impressions which her beauty had made upon him and the great delight he took in it, <reference osisRef="Song.6.11-Song.6.13">ver. 11-13</reference>.
entries.9d530e550370b994cd62be5cea4db53afed4643e: <div eID="gen15319" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15318" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Enquiring after Christ.</title> <div sID="gen15320" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Whither is thy beloved gone, O thou fairest among women? whither is thy beloved turned aside? that we may seek him with thee. <hi type="super">2</hi> My beloved is gone down into his garden, to the beds of spices, to feed in the gardens, and to gather lilies. 3 I <hi type="italic">am</hi> my beloved's, and my beloved <hi type="italic">is</hi> mine: he feedeth among the lilies. <div eID="gen15320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15321" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The enquiry which the daughters of Jerusalem made concerning Christ, <reference osisRef="Song.6.1">v. 1</reference>. They still continue their high thoughts of the church, and call her, as before, the <hi type="italic">fairest among women;</hi> for true sanctity is true beauty. And now they raise their thoughts higher concerning Christ: <hi type="italic">Whither has thy beloved gone, that we may seek him with thee?</hi> This would be but an indecent, unacceptable, compliment, if the song were not to be understood spiritually; for love is jealous of a rival, would monopolize the beloved, and cares not that others should join in seeking him; but those that truly love Christ are desirous that others should love him too, and be joined to him; nay, the greatest instance of duty and respect that the church's children can show to their mother is to join with her in seeking Christ. The <hi type="italic">daughters of Jerusalem,</hi> who had asked (<reference osisRef="Song.5.9">ch. v. 9</reference>), <hi type="italic">What is thy beloved more than another beloved?</hi> wondering that the spouse should be so passionately in love with him, are now of another mind, and are themselves in love with him; for, 1. The spouse had described him, and shown them his excellencies and perfections; and therefore, though they have not seen him, yet, believing, they love him. Those that undervalue Christ do so because they do not know him; when God, by his word and Spirit, discovers him to the soul, with that ray of light the fire of love to him will be kindled. 2. The spouse had expressed her own love to him, her rest in that love, and triumphed in it: <hi type="italic">This is my beloved;</hi> and that flame in her breast scattered sparks into theirs. As sinful lusts, when they break out, defile many, so the pious zeal of some may <hi type="italic">provoke many,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.2">2 Cor. ix. 2</reference>. 3. The spouse had bespoken their help in seeking her beloved (<reference osisRef="Song.5.8">ch. v. 8</reference>); but now they beg hers, for they perceive that now the cloud she had been under began to scatter, and the sky to clear up, and, while she was describing her beloved to them, she herself retrieved her comfort in him. Drooping Christians would find benefit themselves by talking of Christ, as well as do good to others. Now here, (1.) They enquire concerning him, "<hi type="italic">Wither has thy beloved gone?</hi> which way must we steer our course in pursuit of him?" Note, Those that are made acquainted with the excellencies of Christ, and the comfort of an interest in him, cannot but be inquisitive after him and desirous to know where they may meet with him. (2.) They offer their service to the spouse to accompany her in quest of him: <hi type="italic">We will seek him with thee.</hi> Those that would find Christ must seek him, seek him early, seek him diligently; and it is best seeking Christ in concert, to join with those that are seeking him. We must seek for communion with Christ in communion with saints. We know <hi type="italic">whither our beloved has gone;</hi> he has gone to heaven, <hi type="italic">to his Father, and our Father.</hi> He took care to send us notice of it, that we might know how to direct to him, <reference osisRef="John.20.17">John xx. 17</reference>. We must by faith see him there, and by prayer seek him there, with boldness <hi type="italic">enter into the holiest,</hi> and herein must join with <hi type="italic">the generation of those that seek him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.24.6">Ps. xxiv. 6</reference>), even with <hi type="italic">all that in every place call upon him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.2">1 Cor. i. 2</reference>. We must pray with and for others. <div eID="gen15321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15322" type="x-p"/> II. The answer which the spouse gave to this enquiry, <reference osisRef="Song.6.2-Song.6.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. Now she complains not any more, as she had done (<reference osisRef="Song.5.6">ch. v. 6</reference>), "He is gone, he is gone," that she knew not where to find him, or doubted she had lost him for ever; no, <div eID="gen15322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15323" type="x-p"/> 1. Now she knows very well where he is (<reference osisRef="Song.6.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">My beloved</hi> is not to be found in the streets of the city, and the crowd and noise that are there; there I have in vain looked for him" (as his parents <hi type="italic">sought him among their kindred and acquaintance, and found him not</hi>); "but he <hi type="italic">has gone down to his garden,</hi> a place of privacy and retirement." The more we withdraw from the hurry of the world the more likely we are to have acquaintance with Christ, who took his disciples into a garden, there to be witnesses of the agonies of his love. Christ's church is a garden enclosed, and separated from the open common of the world; it is <hi type="italic">his garden,</hi> which he has planted as he did the garden of Eden, which he takes care of, and delights in. Though he had gone up to the paradise above, yet he comes down to his garden on earth; it lies low, but he condescends to visit it, and wonderful condescension it is. <hi type="italic">Will God in very deed dwell with man upon the earth?</hi> Those that would find Christ may expect to meet with him <hi type="italic">in his garden</hi> the church, for <hi type="italic">there he records his name</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.20.24">Exod. xx. 24</reference>); they must attend upon him in the ordinances which he has instituted, the word, sacraments, and prayer, wherein he will be with us <hi type="italic">always, even to the end of the world.</hi> The spouse here refers to what Christ had said (<reference osisRef="Song.5.1">ch. v. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">I have come into my garden.</hi> It is as if she had said, "What a fool was I to fret and fatigue myself in seeking him where he was not, when he himself had told me where he was!" Words of direction and comfort are often out of the way when we have occasion to use them, till the blessed Spirit brings them to our remembrance, and then we wonder how we overlooked them. Christ has told us that he would <hi type="italic">come into his garden;</hi> thither therefore we must go to seek him. <hi type="italic">The beds,</hi> and smaller <hi type="italic">gardens,</hi> in this greater, are the particular churches, the <hi type="italic">synagogues of God in the land</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.84.8">Ps. lxxxiv. 8</reference>); the <hi type="italic">spices</hi> and <hi type="italic">lilies</hi> are particular believers, the planting of the Lord, and pleasant in his eyes. When Christ comes down to his church it is, (1.) <hi type="italic">To feed</hi> among <hi type="italic">the gardens,</hi> to feed his flock, which he feeds not, as other shepherds, in the open fields, but in his garden, so well are they provided for, <reference osisRef="Ps.23.2">Ps. xxiii. 2</reference>. He comes to feed his friends, and entertain them; there you may not only find him, but find his table richly furnished, and a hearty welcome to it. He comes to feed himself, that is, to please himself with the products of his own grace in his people; <hi type="italic">for the Lord takes pleasure in those that fear him.</hi> He has many gardens, many particular churches of different sizes and shapes; but, while they are his, he feeds in them all, manifests himself among them, and is well pleased with them. (2.) <hi type="italic">To gather lilies,</hi> wherewith he is pleased to entertain and adorn himself. He picks the lilies one by one, and gathers them to himself; and there will be a general harvest of them at the great day, when he will send forth his angels, to gather all his lilies, that he may be for ever glorified and admired in them. <div eID="gen15323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15324" type="x-p"/> 2. She is very confident of her own interest in him (<reference osisRef="Song.6.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I am my beloved's, and my beloved is mine;</hi> the relation is mutual, and the knot is tied, which cannot be loosed; for <hi type="italic">he feeds among the lilies,</hi> and my communion with him is a certain token of my interest in him." She had said this before (<reference osisRef="Song.2.16">ch. ii. 16</reference>); but, (1.) Here she repeats it as that which she resolved to abide by, and which she took an unspeakable pleasure and satisfaction in; she liked her choice too well to change. Our communion with God is very much maintained and kept up by the frequent renewing of our covenant with him and rejoicing in it. (2.) She had occasion to repeat it, for she had acted unkindly to her beloved, and, for her so doing, he had justly withdrawn himself from her, and therefore there was occasion to take fresh hold of the covenant, which continues firm between Christ and believes, notwithstanding their failings and his frowns, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.30-Ps.89.35">Ps. lxxxix. 30-35</reference>. "I have been careless and wanting in my duty, and yet <hi type="italic">I am my beloved's;</hi>" for every transgression in the covenant does not throw us out of covenant. "He has justly hidden his face from me and denied me his comforts, and yet <hi type="italic">my beloved is mine;</hi>" for rebukes and chastenings are not only consistent with, but they flow from covenant-love. (3.) When we have not a full assurance of Christ's love we must live by a faithful adherence to him. "Though I have not the sensible consolation I used to have, yet I will cleave to this, <hi type="italic">Christ is mine and I am his.</hi>" (4.) Though she had said the same before, yet now she inverts the order, and asserts her interest in her first: <hi type="italic">I am my beloved's,</hi> entirely devoted and dedicated to him; and then her interest in him and in his grace: "<hi type="italic">My beloved is mine,</hi> and I am happy, truly happy in him." If our own hearts can but witness for us that we are his, there is no room left to question his being ours; for the covenant never breaks on his side. (5.) It is now her comfort, as it was then, that <hi type="italic">he feeds among the lilies,</hi> that he takes delight in his people and converses freely with them, as we do with those with whom we feed; and therefore, though at present he be withdrawn, "I shall meet with him again. <hi type="italic">I shall yet praise him who is the health of my countenance, and my God.</hi>"
entries.565e8b0d1257b4397290c85d696ea10813c1986a: <div eID="gen15324" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Church's Confidence in Christ; The Love of Christ to the Church.</title> <div sID="gen15325" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> beautiful, O my love, as Tirzah, comely as Jerusalem, terrible as <hi type="italic">an army</hi> with banners. <hi type="super">5</hi> Turn away thine eyes from me, for they have overcome me: thy hair <hi type="italic">is</hi> as a flock of goats that appear from Gilead. <hi type="super">6</hi> Thy teeth <hi type="italic">are</hi> as a flock of sheep which go up from the washing, whereof every one beareth twins, and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> not one barren among them. <hi type="super">7</hi> As a piece of a pomegranate <hi type="italic">are</hi> thy temples within thy locks. <hi type="super">8</hi> There are threescore queens, and fourscore concubines, and virgins without number. <hi type="super">9</hi> My dove, my undefiled is <hi type="italic">but</hi> one; she <hi type="italic">is</hi> the <hi type="italic">only</hi> one of her mother, she <hi type="italic">is</hi> the choice <hi type="italic">one</hi> of her that bare her. The daughters saw her, and blessed her; <hi type="italic">yea,</hi> the queens and the concubines, and they praised her. <hi type="super">10</hi> Who <hi type="italic">is</hi> she <hi type="italic">that</hi> looketh forth as the morning, fair as the moon, clear as the sun, <hi type="italic">and</hi> terrible as <hi type="italic">an army</hi> with banners? <div eID="gen15325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15326" type="x-p"/> Now we must suppose Christ graciously returned to his spouse, from whom he had withdrawn himself, returned to converse with her (for he speaks to her and <hi type="italic">makes her to hear joy and gladness</hi>), returned to favour her, having forgiven and forgotten all her unkindness, for he speaks very tenderly and respectfully to her. <div eID="gen15326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15327" type="x-p"/> I. He pronounces her truly amiable (<reference osisRef="Song.6.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou art beautiful, O my love! as Tirzah,</hi> a city in the tribe of Manasseh, whose name signifies <hi type="italic">pleasant,</hi> or <hi type="italic">acceptable,</hi> the situation, no doubt, being very happy and the building fine and uniform. <hi type="italic">Thou art comely as Jerusalem,</hi> a city <hi type="italic">compact together</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.122.3">Ps. cxxii. 3</reference>), and which Solomon had built and beautified, <hi type="italic">the joy of the whole earth;</hi> it was an honour to the world (whether they thought so or no) that there was such a city in it. It was the holy city, and that was the greatest beauty of it; and fitly is the church compared to it, for it was figured and typified by it. The gospel-church is <hi type="italic">the Jerusalem that is above</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.26">Gal. iv. 26</reference>), <hi type="italic">the heavenly Jerusalem</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.22">Heb. xii. 22</reference>); in it God has <hi type="italic">his sanctuary,</hi> and is, in a special manner, present; thence he has the tribute of praise issuing; it is his rest for ever, and therefore it is <hi type="italic">comely as Jerusalem,</hi> and, being so, is <hi type="italic">terrible as an army with banners.</hi> Church-censures, duly administered, strike an awe upon men's consciences; the word (the weapons of her warfare) <hi type="italic">casts down imaginations</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.10.5">2 Cor. x. 5</reference>), and even an unbeliever is convinced and judged by the solemnity of holy ordinances, <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.24-1Cor.14.25">1 Cor. xiv. 24, 25</reference>. The saints by faith <hi type="italic">overcome the world</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.5.4">1 John v. 4</reference>); nay, like Jacob, they have <hi type="italic">power with God and prevail,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.32.28">Gen. xxxii. 28</reference>. <div eID="gen15327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15328" type="x-p"/> II. He owns himself in love with her, <reference osisRef="Song.6.5">v. 5</reference>. Though, for a small moment, and in a little wrath, he had hid his face from her, yet now he gathers her with very surprising instances of <hi type="italic">everlasting lovingkindness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.54.8">Isa. liv. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">Turn thy eyes towards me</hi> (so some read it), "turn the eyes of faith and love towards me, <hi type="italic">for they have lifted me up;</hi> look unto me, and be comforted." When we are calling to God to turn the eye of his favour towards us he is calling to us to turn the eye of our obedience towards him. We read it as a strange expression of love, "<hi type="italic">Turn away thy eyes from me, for</hi> I cannot bear the brightness of them; <hi type="italic">they have</hi> quite <hi type="italic">overcome me,</hi> and I am prevailed with to overlook all that is past;" as God said to Moses, when he interceded for Israel, "<hi type="italic">Let me alone,</hi> or I must yield," <reference osisRef="Exod.32.10">Exod. xxxii. 10</reference>. Christ is pleased to borrow these expressions of a passionate lover only to express the tenderness of a compassionate Redeemer, and the delight he takes in his redeemed and in the workings of his own grace in them. <div eID="gen15328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15329" type="x-p"/> III. He repeats, almost word for word, part of the description he had given of her beauty (<reference osisRef="Song.4.1-Song.4.3">ch. iv. 1-3</reference>), her <hi type="italic">hair,</hi> her <hi type="italic">teeth,</hi> her <hi type="italic">temples</hi> (<reference osisRef="Song.6.5-Song.6.7">v. 5-7</reference>), not because he could not have described it in other words, and by other similitudes, but to show that he had still the same esteem for her since her unkindness to him, and his withdrawings from her, that he had before. Lest she should think that, though he would not quite cast her off, yet he would think the worse of her while he knew her, he says the same of her now that he had done; for those <hi type="italic">to whom much is forgiven will love the more,</hi> and, consequently, will be the more loved, for Christ has said, <hi type="italic">I love those that love me.</hi> He is pleased with his people, notwithstanding their weaknesses, when they sincerely repent of them and return to their duty, and commends them as if they had already arrived at perfection. <div eID="gen15329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15330" type="x-p"/> IV. He prefers her before all competitors, and sees all the beauties and perfections of others meeting and centering in her (<reference osisRef="Song.6.8-Song.6.9">v. 8, 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">There are,</hi> it may be, <hi type="italic">threescore queens,</hi> who, like Esther, have by their beauty attained to the royal state and dignity, <hi type="italic">and fourscore concubines,</hi> whom kings have preferred before their own queens, as more charming, and these attended by their maids of honour, <hi type="italic">virgins without number,</hi> who, when there is a ball at court, appear in great splendour, with beauty that dazzles the eyes of the spectators; but <hi type="italic">my dove, my undefiled, is but one,</hi> a holy one." 1. She excels them all. Go through all the world, and view the societies of men that reckon themselves wise and happy, kingdoms, courts, senates, councils, or whatever incorporations you may think valuable, they are none of them to be compared with the church of Christ; their honours and beauties are nothing to hers. <hi type="italic">Who is like unto thee, O Israel!</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.33.29">Deut. xxxiii. 29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.4.6-Deut.4.7">iv. 6, 7</reference>. There are particular persons, as <hi type="italic">virgins without number,</hi> who are famed for their accomplishments, the beauties of their address, language, and performances, but the beauty of holiness is beyond all other beauty: "<hi type="italic">My dove, my undefiled, is one,</hi> has that one beauty that she is a dove, an undefiled dove, and mine, and that makes her excel the queens and virgins, though they were ever so many." 2. She included them all. "Other kings have many queens, and concubines, and virgins, with whose conversation they entertain themselves, but <hi type="italic">my dove, my undefiled,</hi> is to me instead of all; in that one I have more than they have in all theirs." Or, "Though there are many particular churches, some of greater dignity, others of less, some of longer, others of shorter, standing, and many particular believers, of different gifts and attainments, some more eminent, others less so, yet they all constitute but one catholic church, are all but parts of that whole, and that is <hi type="italic">my dove, my undefiled.</hi>" Christ is the centre of the church's unity; all the children of God that are scattered abroad are gathered by him (<reference osisRef="John.11.52">John xi. 52</reference>), and meet in him (<reference osisRef="Eph.1.10">Eph. i. 10</reference>), and are all his doves. <div eID="gen15330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15331" type="x-p"/> V. He shows how much she was esteemed, not by him only, but by all that had acquaintance with her and stood in relation to her. It would add to her praise to say, 1. That she was her mother's darling; she had that in her, from a child, which recommended her to the particular affection of her parents. As Solomon himself is said to have been <hi type="italic">tender and an only one in the sight of his mother</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.3">Prov. iv. 3</reference>), so was she <hi type="italic">the only one of her mother,</hi> as dear as if she had been an only one, and, if there were many more, yet she was <hi type="italic">the choice one of her that bore her,</hi> more excellent than all the societies of men this world ever produced. All the kingdoms of the world, and the glory of them, are nothing, in Christ's account, compared with the church, which is made up of <hi type="italic">the excellent ones of the earth,</hi> the <hi type="italic">precious sons of Zion, comparable to fine gold,</hi> and <hi type="italic">more excellent than their neighbours.</hi> 2. That she was admired by all her acquaintance, not only <hi type="italic">the daughters,</hi> who were her juniors, but even <hi type="italic">the queens and the concubines,</hi> who might have reason to be jealous of her as a rival; <hi type="italic">they</hi> all <hi type="italic">blessed her,</hi> and wished well to her, <hi type="italic">praised her,</hi> and spoke well of her. <hi type="italic">The daughters of Jerusalem</hi> called her the <hi type="italic">fairest among women;</hi> all agreed to give her the pre-eminence for beauty, and every sheaf bowed to hers. Note, (1.) Those that have any correct sense of things cannot but be convinced in their consciences (whatever they say) that godly people are excellent people; many will give them their good word, and more their good-will. (2.) Jesus Christ takes notice what people think and speak of his church, and is well pleased with those that honour such as fear the Lord, and takes it ill of those that despise them, particularly when they are under a cloud, that <hi type="italic">offend any of his little ones.</hi> <div eID="gen15331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15332" type="x-p"/> VI. He produces the encomium that was given of her, and makes it his own (<reference osisRef="Song.6.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">Who is she that looks forth as the morning?</hi> This is applicable both to the church in the world and to grace in the heart. <div eID="gen15332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15333" type="x-p"/> 1. They are amiable as the light, the most beautiful of all visible things. Christians are, or should be, the lights of the world. The patriarchal church <hi type="italic">looked forth as the morning</hi> when the promise of the Messiah was first made known, and <hi type="italic">the day-spring from on high visited</hi> this dark world. The Jewish church was <hi type="italic">fair as the moon;</hi> the ceremonial law was an imperfect light; it shone by reflection; it was changing as the moon, did not make day, nor had <hi type="italic">the sun of righteousness yet risen.</hi> But the Christian church is clear <hi type="italic">as the sun,</hi> exhibits a great <hi type="italic">light to those that sat in darkness.</hi> Or we may apply it to the kingdom of grace, the gospel-kingdom. (1.) In its rise, it <hi type="italic">looks forth as the morning</hi> after a dark night; it is discovering (<reference osisRef="Job.38.12-Job.38.13">Job xxxviii. 12, 13</reference>), and very acceptable, <hi type="italic">looks forth</hi> pleasantly as a clear morning; but it is small in its beginnings, and scarcely perceptible at first. (2.) It is, at the best, in this world, but <hi type="italic">fair as the moon,</hi> which shines with a borrowed light, which has her changes and eclipses, and her spots too, and, when at the full, does but rule by night. But, (3.) When it is perfected in the kingdom of glory then it will be <hi type="italic">clear as the sun,</hi> the church <hi type="italic">clothed with the sun,</hi> with Christ <hi type="italic">the sun of righteousness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.12.1">Rev. xii. 1</reference>. Those that love God will then be <hi type="italic">as the sun when he goes forth in his strength</hi> (<reference osisRef="Judg.5.31">Judges v. 31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.13.43">Matt. xiii. 43</reference>); they shall shine in inexpressible glory, and that which is perfect will then come; there shall be no darkness, no spots, <reference osisRef="Isa.30.26">Isa. xxx. 26</reference>. <div eID="gen15333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15334" type="x-p"/> 2. The beauty of the church and of believers is not only amiable, but <hi type="italic">awful as an army with banners.</hi> The church, in this world, is <hi type="italic">as an army,</hi> as the camp of Israel in the wilderness; its state is militant; it is in the midst of enemies, and is engaged in a constant conflict with them. Believers are soldiers in this army. It has its <hi type="italic">banners;</hi> the gospel of Christ is an ensign (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.12">Isa. xi. 12</reference>), the love of Christ, <reference osisRef="Song.2.4">ch. ii. 4</reference>. It is marshalled, and kept in order and under discipline. It is <hi type="italic">terrible</hi> to its enemies as Israel in the wilderness was, <reference osisRef="Exod.15.14">Exod. xv. 14</reference>. When Balaam saw Israel encamped according to their tribes, by their standards, with colours displayed, he said, <hi type="italic">How goodly are thy tents, O Jacob!</hi> <reference osisRef="Num.24.5">Num. xxiv. 5</reference>. When the church preserves her purity she secures her honour and victory; when she is <hi type="italic">fair as the moon,</hi> and <hi type="italic">clear as the sun,</hi> she is truly great and formidable.
entries.4c98626e26da03d884eeb0ec3d6ebb93baa536a4: <div eID="gen15334" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Love of Christ to the Church.</title> <div sID="gen15335" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> I went down into the garden of nuts to see the fruits of the valley, <hi type="italic">and</hi> to see whether the vine flourished, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the pomegranates budded. <hi type="super">12</hi> Or ever I was aware, my soul made me <hi type="italic">like</hi> the chariots of Amminadib. 13 Return, return, O Shulamite; return, return, that we may look upon thee. What will ye see in the Shulamite? As it were the company of two armies. <div eID="gen15335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15336" type="x-p"/> Christ having now returned to his spouse, and the breach being entirely made up, and the falling out of these lovers being the renewing of love, Christ here gives an account both of the distance and of the reconciliation. <div eID="gen15336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15337" type="x-p"/> I. That when he had withdrawn from his church as his spouse, and did not comfort her, yet even then he had his eye upon it as his garden, which he took care of (<reference osisRef="Song.6.11">v. 11</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I went down into the garden of nuts,</hi> or nutmegs, <hi type="italic">to see the fruits of the valley,</hi> with complacency and concern, to see them as my own." When he was out of sight he was no further off than the garden, hid among the trees of the garden, in a low and dark valley; but then he was observing <hi type="italic">how the vine flourished,</hi> that he might do all that to it which was necessary to promote its flourishing, and might delight himself in it as a man does in a fruitful garden. He went to see whether <hi type="italic">the pomegranates budded.</hi> Christ observes the first beginnings of the good work of grace in the soul and the early buddings of devout affections and inclinations there, and is well pleased with them, as we are with the blossoms of the spring. <div eID="gen15337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15338" type="x-p"/> II. That yet he could not long content himself with this, but suddenly felt a powerful, irresistible, inclination in his own bosom to return to his church, as his spouse, being moved with her lamentations after him, and her languishing desire towards him (<reference osisRef="Song.6.12">v. 12</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Or ever I was aware, my soul made me like the chariots of Ammi-nadib;</hi> I could not any longer keep at a distance; my repentings were kindled together, and I presently resolved to fly back to the arms of my love, my dove." Thus Joseph made himself strange to his brethren, for a while, to chastise them for their former unkindnesses, and make trial of their present temper, till he could no longer refrain himself, but, <hi type="italic">or ever he was aware,</hi> burst out into tears, and said, <hi type="italic">I am Joseph,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.45.1">Gen. xlv. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.45.3">3</reference>. And now the spouse perceives, as David did (<reference osisRef="Ps.31.22">Ps. xxxi. 22</reference>), that though she <hi type="italic">said in her haste, I am cut off from before thy eyes,</hi> yet, at the same time, he <hi type="italic">heard the voice of her supplications,</hi> and became <hi type="italic">like the chariots of Ammi-nadib,</hi> which were noted for their beauty and swiftness. <hi type="italic">My soul put me into the chariots of my willing people</hi> (so some read it), "the chariots of their faith, and hope, and love, their desires, and prayers, and expectations, which they sent after me, to fetch me back, as chariots of fire with horses of fire." Note, 1. Christ's people are, and ought to be, a willing people. 2. If they continue seeking Christ and longing after him, even when he seems to withdraw from them, he will graciously return to them in due time, perhaps sooner than they think and with a pleasing surprise. No chariots sent for Christ shall return empty. 3. All Christ's gracious returns to his people take rise from himself. It is not they, it is his own soul, that puts him into the chariots of his people; for he is gracious because he will be gracious, and loves his Israel because he would love them; not for their sakes, be it known to them. <div eID="gen15338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15339" type="x-p"/> III. That he, having returned to her, kindly courted her return to him, notwithstanding the discouragements she laboured under. Let her not despair of obtaining as much comfort as ever she had before this distance happened, but take the comfort of the return of her beloved, <reference osisRef="Song.6.13">v. 13</reference>. Here, 1. The church is called <hi type="italic">Shulamite,</hi> referring either to <hi type="italic">Solomon,</hi> the bridegroom in type, by whose name she is called, in token of her relation to him and union with him (thus believers are called <hi type="italic">Christians</hi> from <hi type="italic">Christ</hi>), or referring to <hi type="italic">Salem,</hi> the place of her birth and residence, as the woman of <hi type="italic">Shunem</hi> is called the <hi type="italic">Shunamite.</hi> Heaven is the Salem whence the saints have their birth, and where they have their citizenship; those that belong to Christ, and are bound for heaven, shall be called <hi type="italic">Shulamites.</hi> 2. She is invited to return, and the invitation most earnestly pressed: <hi type="italic">Return, return;</hi> and again, "<hi type="italic">Return, return;</hi> recover the peace thou hast lost and forfeited; come back to thy former composedness and cheerfulness of spirit." Note, Good Christians, after they have had their comfort disturbed, are sometimes hard to be pacified, and need to be earnestly persuaded to return again to their rest. As revolting sinners have need to be called to again and again (<hi type="italic">Turn you, turn you, why will you die?</hi>) so disquieted saints have need to be called to again and again, <hi type="italic">Turn you, turn you,</hi> why will you droop; <hi type="italic">Why art thou cast down, O my soul?</hi> 3. Having returned, she is desired to show her face: <hi type="italic">That we may look upon thee.</hi> Go no longer with thy face covered like a mourner. Let those that have made their peace with God <hi type="italic">lift up their faces without spot</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.22.26">Job xxii. 26</reference>); let them come boldly to his throne of grace. Christ is pleased with the cheerfulness and humble confidence of his people, and would have them look pleasant. "Let us <hi type="italic">look upon thee,</hi> not I only, but the holy angels, who rejoice in the consolation of saints as well as in the conversion of sinners; not I only, but all the daughters." Christ and believers are pleased with the beauty of the church. 4. A short account is given of what is to be seen in her. The question is asked, <hi type="italic">What will you see in the Shulamite?</hi> And it is answered, <hi type="italic">As it were the company of two armies.</hi> (1.) Some think she gives this account of herself; she is shy of appearing, unwilling to be looked upon, having, in her own account, no form or comeliness. Alas! says she, <hi type="italic">What will you see in the Shulamite?</hi> nothing that is worth your looking upon, nothing but <hi type="italic">as it were the company of two armies</hi> actually engaged, where nothing is to be seen but blood and slaughter. The watchmen had smitten her, and wounded her, and she carried in her face the marks of those wounds, looked as if she had been fighting. She had said (<reference osisRef="Song.1.6">ch. i. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">Look not upon me because I am black;</hi> here she says, "Look not upon me because I am bloody." Or it may denote the constant struggle that is between grace and corruption in the souls of believers; they are in them <hi type="italic">as two armies</hi> continually skirmishing, which makes her ashamed to show her face. (2.) Others think her beloved gives the account of her. "I will tell you what you shall <hi type="italic">see in the Shulamite;</hi> you shall see as noble a sight as that of two armies, or two parts of the same army, drawn out in rank and file; not only <hi type="italic">as an army with banners,</hi> but as <hi type="italic">two armies,</hi> with a majesty double to what was before spoken; she is as <hi type="italic">Mahanaim,</hi> as the two hosts which Jacob saw (<reference osisRef="Gen.32.1-Gen.32.2">Gen. xxxii. 1, 2</reference>), a host of saints and a host of angels ministering to them; the church militant, the church triumphant." Behold <hi type="italic">two armies;</hi> in both the church appears beautiful.  <chapter eID="Song.6"/> <div eID="gen15339" type="x-p"/>

entries.89314e7d1fdfd738bac1480e59ae3e2398997dfc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8269"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 6</title> <div sID="gen13083" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Song.6.1-Song.6.13">So 6:1-13</reference>.<div eID="gen13083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13084" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8269"/>1. Historically, at Jesus Christ's crucifixion and burial, Joseph of Arimathea, and Nicodemus, and others, joined with His professed disciples. By speaking of Jesus Christ, the bride does good not only to her own soul, but to others (see on <reference osisRef="Song.1.4">So 1:4</reference>; Mal 3:16; <reference osisRef="Matt.5.14-Matt.5.16">Mt 5:14-16</reference>). Compare the hypocritical use of similar words (<reference osisRef="Matt.2.8">Mt 2:8</reference>). <div eID="gen13084" type="x-p"/>
entries.e35db8ad49cc09d003da91bc6850db6f86604e9b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8270"/><div sID="gen13085" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8270"/><hi type="bold">2. gone down--</hi>Jerusalem was on a hill (answering to its moral elevation), and the gardens were at a little distance in the valleys below.<div eID="gen13085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13086" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beds of spices--</hi>(balsam) which He Himself calls the "mountain of myrrh," &c. (<reference osisRef="Song.4.6">So 4:6</reference>), and again (<reference osisRef="Song.8.14">So 8:14</reference>), the resting-place of His body amidst spices, and of His soul in paradise, and now in heaven, where He stands as High Priest for ever. Nowhere else in the Song is there mention of mountains of spices.<div eID="gen13086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13087" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">feed in ... gardens--</hi>that is, in the churches, though He may have withdrawn for a time from the individual believer: she implies an invitation to the daughters of Jerusalem to enter His spiritual Church, and become lilies, made white by His blood. He is gathering some lilies now to plant on earth, others to transplant into heaven (<reference osisRef="Song.5.1">So 5:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.5.24">Ge 5:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.4.28">Mr 4:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.4.29">29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.7.60">Ac 7:60</reference>). <div eID="gen13087" type="x-p"/>
entries.8771cc8ee29add4e20213455fa1fe160a2bfb749: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8271"/><div sID="gen13088" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8271"/>3. In speaking of Jesus Christ to others, she regains her own assurance. Literally, "I am for my beloved ... for me." Reverse order from <reference osisRef="Song.2.16">So 2:16</reference>. She now, after the season of darkness, grounds her convictions on His love towards her, more than on hers towards Him (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.3">De 33:3</reference>). There, it was the young believer concluding that she was His, from the sensible assurance that He was hers. <div eID="gen13088" type="x-p"/>
entries.decebcafe460e2cac6358fd4e9c8b7c22154356a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8272"/><div sID="gen13089" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8272"/><hi type="bold">4. Tirzah--</hi>meaning "pleasant" (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.21">He 13:21</reference>); "well-pleasing" (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.14">Mt 5:14</reference>); the royal city of one of the old Canaanite kings (<reference osisRef="Josh.12.24">Jos 12:24</reference>); and after the revolt of Israel, the royal city of its kings, before Omri founded Samaria (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.8">1Ki 16:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.15">15</reference>). No ground for assigning a later date than the time of Solomon to the Song, as Tirzah was even in his time the capital of the north (Israel), as Jerusalem was of the south (Judah).<div eID="gen13089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13090" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Jerusalem--</hi>residence of the kings of Judah, as Tirzah, of Israel (<reference osisRef="Ps.48.1">Psa 48:1</reference>, &c.; 122:1-3; 125:1, 2). Loveliness, security, unity, and loyalty; also the union of Israel and Judah in the Church (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.13">Is 11:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.18">Jr 3:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.16">Eze 37:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.17.22">17, 22</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Heb.12.22">He 12:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.21.2">Re 21:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.12">12</reference>).<div eID="gen13090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13091" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">terrible--</hi>awe-inspiring. Not only armed as a city on the defensive, but as an army on the offensive.<div eID="gen13091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13092" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">banners--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Song.5.10">So 5:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.60.4">Psa 60:4</reference>); Jehovah-nissi (<reference osisRef="2Cor.10.4">2Co 10:4</reference>). <div eID="gen13092" type="x-p"/>
entries.4f9426a9c8d1e5e6a2ae5af70074b77ff0610362: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8273"/><div sID="gen13093" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8273"/>5. (<reference osisRef="Song.4.9">So 4:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.32.28">Ge 32:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.32.9-Exod.32.14">Ex 32:9-14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.12.4">Ho 12:4</reference>). This is the way "the army" (<reference osisRef="Song.6.4">So 6:4</reference>) "overcomes" not only enemies, but Jesus Christ Himself, with eyes fixed on Him (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.15">Psa 25:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.11.12">Mt 11:12</reference>). Historically, <reference osisRef="Song.6.3-Song.6.5">So 6:3-5</reference>, represent the restoration of Jesus Christ to His Church at the resurrection; His sending her forth as an army, with new powers (Mr 16:15-18, 20); His rehearsing the same instructions (see on <reference osisRef="Song.6.6">So 6:6</reference>) as when with them (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.44">Lu 24:44</reference>).<div eID="gen13093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13094" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">overcome--</hi>literally, "have taken me by storm." <div eID="gen13094" type="x-p"/>
entries.2a7ba04cd5fcd06789cb79a45dc50a018ddead7a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8274"/><div sID="gen13095" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8274"/>6. Not vain repetition of <reference osisRef="Song.4.1">So 4:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.2">2</reference>. The use of the same words shows His love unchanged after her temporary unfaithfulness (Mal 3:6). <div eID="gen13095" type="x-p"/>
entries.950ca805ae578eec4c33c551825808d80d7ad6d4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8275"/><div sID="gen13096" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8275"/><hi type="bold">8. threescore--</hi>indefinite number, as in <reference osisRef="Song.3.7">So 3:7</reference>. Not queens, &c., of Solomon, but witnesses of the espousals, rulers of the earth contrasted with the saints, who, though many, are but "one" bride (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.15">Is 52:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.22.25">Lu 22:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.22.26">26</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.17.21">Joh 17:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.17">1Co 10:17</reference>). The one Bride is contrasted with the many wives whom Eastern kings had in violation of the marriage law (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.1-1Kgs.11.3">1Ki 11:1-3</reference>). <div eID="gen13096" type="x-p"/>
entries.618f92365e7287a418712d6b09a424a46ae065a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8276"/><div sID="gen13097" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8276"/>9. Hollow professors, like half wives, have no part in the one bride.<div eID="gen13097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13098" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">only one of her mother--</hi>namely, "Jerusalem above" (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.26">Ga 4:26</reference>). The "little sister" (<reference osisRef="Song.8.8">So 8:8</reference>) is not inconsistent with her being "the only one"; for that sister is one with herself (<reference osisRef="John.10.16">Joh 10:16</reference>).<div eID="gen13098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13099" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">choice--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Eph.1.4">Ep 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.13">2Th 2:13</reference>). As she exalted Him above all others (<reference osisRef="Song.5.10">So 5:10</reference>), so He now her.<div eID="gen13099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13100" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">daughters ... blessed her--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.8.18">Is 8:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.61.9">61:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.14">Eze 16:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Thess.1.10">2Th 1:10</reference>). So at her appearance after Pentecost (<reference osisRef="Acts.4.13">Ac 4:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.6.15">6:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.24.25">24:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.26.28">26:28</reference>). <div eID="gen13100" type="x-p"/>
entries.b4ad8147ffc136861a99d9d3e53f96c5cc8c10d9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8277"/><div sID="gen13101" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8277"/>10. The words expressing the admiration of the daughters. Historically (<reference osisRef="Acts.5.24-Acts.5.39">Ac 5:24-39</reference>).<div eID="gen13101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13102" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as the morning--</hi>As yet she is not come to the fulness of her light (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.18">Pr 4:18</reference>).<div eID="gen13102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13103" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">moon--</hi>shining in the night, by light borrowed from the sun; so the bride, in the darkness of this world, reflects the light of the Sun of righteousness (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">2Co 3:18</reference>).<div eID="gen13103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13104" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sun--</hi>Her light of justification is perfect, for it is His (<reference osisRef="2Cor.5.21">2Co 5:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.4.17">1Jo 4:17</reference>). The moon has less light, and has only one half illuminated; so the bride's sanctification is as yet imperfect. Her future glory (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.43">Mt 13:43</reference>).<div eID="gen13104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13105" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">army--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Song.6.4">So 6:4</reference>). The climax requires this to be applied to the starry and angelic hosts, from which God is called Lord of Sabaoth. Her final glory (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.5">Ge 15:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.12.3">Da 12:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.12.1">Re 12:1</reference>). The Church Patriarchal, "the morning"; Levitical, "the moon"; Evangelical, "the sun"; Triumphant, "the bannered army" (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.14">Re 19:14</reference>). <div eID="gen13105" type="x-p"/>
entries.1bd3bf17f3b9219418c69c695b2491deaaaba57c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8278"/><div sID="gen13106" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8278"/>11. The bride's words; for she everywhere is the narrator, and often soliloquizes, which He never does. The first garden (<reference osisRef="Song.2.11-Song.2.13">So 2:11-13</reference>) was that of spring, full of flowers and grapes not yet ripe; the second, autumn, with spices (which are always connected with the person of Jesus Christ), and nothing unripe (<reference osisRef="Song.4.13">So 4:13</reference>, &c.). The third here, of "nuts," from the previous autumn; the end of winter, and verge of spring; the Church in the upper room (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.13">Ac 1:13</reference>, &c.), when one dispensation was just closed, the other not yet begun; the hard shell of the old needing to be broken, and its inner sweet kernel extracted [Origen] (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.27">Lu 24:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.32">32</reference>); waiting for the Holy Ghost to usher in spiritual spring. The walnut is meant, with a bitter outer husk, a hard shell, and sweet kernel. So the Word is distasteful to the careless; when awakened, the sinner finds the letter hard, until the Holy Ghost reveals the sweet inner spirit.<div eID="gen13106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13107" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fruits of the Valley--</hi>Maurer translates, "the blooming products of the river," that is, the plants growing on the margin of the river flowing through the garden. She goes to watch the first sproutings of the various plants. <div eID="gen13107" type="x-p"/>
entries.73c9eda7eda2c897aae5d82b2535533df37d068b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8279"/><div sID="gen13108" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8279"/>12. Sudden outpourings of the Spirit on Pentecost (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.1-Acts.2.13">Ac 2:1-13</reference>), while the Church was using the means (answering to "the garden," <reference osisRef="Song.6.11">So 6:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.3.8">Joh 3:8</reference>).<div eID="gen13108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13109" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ammi-nadib--</hi>supposed to me one proverbial for swift driving. Similarly (<reference osisRef="Song.1.9">So 1:9</reference>). Rather, "my willing people" (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.3">Psa 110:3</reference>). A willing chariot bore a "willing people"; or Nadib is the Prince, Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.17">Psa 68:17</reference>). She is borne in a moment into His presence (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.6">Ep 2:6</reference>). <div eID="gen13109" type="x-p"/>
entries.2d51a55cf90cfce64f9721f16385cf22cc37bb95: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8280"/><div sID="gen13110" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8280"/>13. Entreaty of the daughters of Jerusalem to her, in her chariot-like flight from them (compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.2.12">2Ki 2:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.19.14">2Sa 19:14</reference>).<div eID="gen13110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13111" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Shulamite--</hi>new name applied to her now for the first time. Feminine of Solomon, Prince of Peace; His bride, daughter of peace, accepting and proclaiming it (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.7">Is 52:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.14.27">Joh 14:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.5.1">Ro 5:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.17">Ep 2:17</reference>). Historically, this name answers to the time when, not without a divine design in it, the young Church met in Solomon's porch (<reference osisRef="Acts.3.11">Ac 3:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.5.12">5:12</reference>). The entreaty, "Return, O Shulamite," answers to the people's desire to keep Peter and John, after the lame man was healed, when they were about to enter the temple. Their reply attributing the glory not to themselves, but to Jesus Christ, answers to the bride's reply here, "What will ye see" in me? "As it were," &c. She accepts the name Shulamite, as truly describing her. But adds, that though "one" (<reference osisRef="Song.6.9">So 6:9</reference>), she is nevertheless "two." Her glories are her Lord's, beaming through her (<reference osisRef="Eph.5.31">Ep 5:31</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.32">32</reference>). The two armies are the family of Jesus Christ in heaven, and that on earth, joined and one with Him; the one militant, the other triumphant. Or Jesus Christ and His ministering angels are one army, the Church the other, both being one (<reference osisRef="John.17.21">Joh 17:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.17.22">22</reference>). Allusion is made to Mahanaim (meaning two hosts), the scene of Jacob's victorious conflict by prayer (<reference osisRef="Gen.32.2">Ge 32:2</reference>, 9, 22-30). Though she is peace, yet she has warfare here, between flesh and spirit within and foes without; her strength, as Jacob's at Mahanaim, is Jesus Christ and His host enlisted on her side by prayer; whence she obtains those graces which raise the admiration of the daughters of Jerusalem. <chapter eID="Song.6"/>

entries.d4c9668a7a53485cfa1419c1fae76bfff7041c05: <div eID="gen26088" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen26089" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen26090" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26090" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen26089" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen26091" type="x-p"/> The companions of the bride inquire after the bridegroom, <reference osisRef="Sol.6.1-Sol.6.3">Sol 6:1-3</reference>. A description of the bride, <reference osisRef="Sol.6.4-Sol.6.13">Sol 6:4-13</reference>. <div eID="gen26091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26092" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen26092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26093" type="x-p"/> Whither is thy beloved gone - These words are supposed to be addressed to the bride by her own companions, and are joined to the preceding chapter by the Hebrew and all the versions.
entries.b4666987b4416fe2e43749d8954407f1063d703d: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen26093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26094" type="x-p"/> My beloved is gone down into his garden - The answer of the bride to her companions.
entries.8ac3fd68834ed2ac7b9490a6e3471da7ad54de91: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen26094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26095" type="x-p"/> Beautiful - as Tirzah - This is supposed to be the address of Solomon to the bride. Tirzah was a city in the tribe of Ephraim, (<reference osisRef="Jos.12.24">Jos 12:24</reference>), and the capital of that district. It appears to have been beautiful in itself, and beautifully situated, for Jeroboam made it his residence before Samaria was built; and it seems to have been the ordinary residence of the kings of Israel, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.17">1Kgs 14:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.21">1Kgs 15:21</reference>. Its same signifies beautiful or delightful. <div eID="gen26095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26096" type="x-p"/> Comely as Jerusalem - This was called the perfection of beauty, <reference osisRef="Psa.48.2">Psa 48:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.48.3">Psa 48:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.50.2">Psa 50:2</reference>. And thus the poet compares the bride's beauty to the two finest places in the land of Palestine, and the capitals of the two kingdoms of Israel and Judah. <div eID="gen26096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26097" type="x-p"/> Terrible as an army with banners - This has been supposed to carry an allusion to the caravans in the East, and the manner in which they are conducted in their travels by night. The caravans are divided into companies, called cottors, according to Thevenet; and each company is distinguished by the form of the brazier in which they carry their lights. After night, these braziers are placed on the ends of long poles, and carried by a person who walks at the head of the company. Some have ten or twelve lights, and are of different forms; some triangular, or like an N; some like an M, by which each pilgrim readily knows his own company, both by night and day. A whole caravan, composed of many thousands of hadgees or pilgrims, divided into various cottors or companies, each having its own distinguishing brazier or light, must necessarily produce a very splendid, if not a terrible, appearance.
entries.87fff7a0db20a716a35b90bc0bdf4656dab6d717: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen26097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26098" type="x-p"/> Turn away thine eyes - As the sight of so many fires after night was extremely dazzling, and the eye could not bear the sight, so the look of the bride was such as pierced the heart, and quite overwhelmed the person who met it. Hence the bridegroom naturally cries out, "Turn away thine eyes from me, for they have overcome me." <div eID="gen26098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26099" type="x-p"/> Thy hair is as a flock of goats - See on <reference osisRef="Sol.4.1">Sol 4:1</reference> (note).
entries.faddeaa2a042bacd28ba1502031eea868a93cca6: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen26099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26100" type="x-p"/> Thy teeth - See on <reference osisRef="Sol.4.2">Sol 4:2</reference> (note).
entries.46f656ecede3672ee71bfb28699ff73ba33db3f0: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen26100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26101" type="x-p"/> As a piece of a pomegranate - See on <reference osisRef="Sol.4.3">Sol 4:3</reference> (note).
entries.3e5f08d136f641953b0b654cb878e6c7f68235f2: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen26101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26102" type="x-p"/> There are threescore queens - Though there be sixty queens, and eighty concubines, or secondary wives, and virgins innumerable, in my harem, yet thou, my dove, my undefiled, art אצת achath, One, the Only One, she in whom I delight beyond all.
entries.301d9fad32d7b3c79f90accc7a76227d7373db91: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen26102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26103" type="x-p"/> The daughters saw her, and blessed her - Not only the Jewish women in general spoke well of her on her arrival, but the queens and concubines praised her as the most accomplished of her sex. <div eID="gen26103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26104" type="x-p"/> With this verse the fourth night of the marriage week is supposed to end.
entries.fffdc78f46039f967d63c15b0c3e902537aafb86: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen26104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26105" type="x-p"/> Looketh forth as the morning - The bride is as lovely as the dawn of day, the Aurora, or perhaps the morning star, Venus. She is even more resplendent, she is as beautiful as the Moon. She even surpasses her, for she is as clear and bright as the Sun; and dangerous withal to look on, for she is as formidable as the vast collection of lights that burn by night at the head of every company in a numerous caravan. See the note on <reference osisRef="Sol.6.4">Sol 6:4</reference> (note). The comparison of a fine woman to the splendor of an unclouded full moon is continually recurring in the writings of the Asiatic poets.
entries.74a9e68d88a54c6de6bc03c0d0b9137578364546: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen26105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26106" type="x-p"/> I went down into the garden of nuts - I believe this and the following verse refer at least to the preparations for a farther consummation of the marriage, or examination of the advancement of the bride's pregnancy. But many circumstances of this kind are so interwoven, and often anticipated and also postponed, that it is exceedingly difficult to arrange the whole so as to ascertain the several parts, and who are the actors and speakers. But other writers find no difficulty here, because they have their system; and that explains all things. <div eID="gen26106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26107" type="x-p"/> It is probably not the hazel but the almond nut, that is referred to here.
entries.95273c7ffaf8804a111bf7d1aedca81ee547cfa5: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen26107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26108" type="x-p"/> The chariots of Amminadib - Probably for their great speed these chariots became proverbial. The passage marks a strong agitation of mind, and something like what we term palpitation of the heart. As I am not aware of any spiritual meaning here, I must be excused from commenting on that which is literal. Amminadib signifies my noble or princely people; but it may here be a proper name, and Amminadib might be celebrated for his skill and rapidity in driving, as Jehu was.
entries.8bbe357e094439d2d35f3486005df18caf324f98: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen26108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26109" type="x-p"/> Return, O Shulamite - This appears to be addressed to the bride, as now the confirmed, acknowledged wife of Solomon; for שולמית shulammith, appears to be a feminine formed from שלמה shelomoh, or Nwmlv shelomon, as we form Charlotte from Charles; Henrietta, from Henry; Janette, from John, etc. <div eID="gen26109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26110" type="x-p"/> The company of two armies - Or the musicians of the camps. She is as terrible as hosts of armed men, on the ground of what is said on <reference osisRef="Sol.6.4">Sol 6:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Sol.6.5">Sol 6:5</reference>. The two armies may refer to the choirs of the bride's virgins, and the bridegroom's companions; but the similitude is not very perceptible. The Targum explains it of "the camps of Israel and Judah:" as if the bridegroom should say, "My beloved possesses all the perfections both of the Israelitish and Jewish women." But how little satisfaction do the best conjectures afford! <div eID="gen26110" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26111" type="x-p"/> With this chapter the fifth night is supposed to end.  <chapter eID="Song.6"/> <div eID="gen26111" type="x-p"/>

entries.6b3aa5cb551e4931ae3a8d00bd11924713d373f2: Sol 6:1 <div eID="gen12642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12643" type="x-p"/> The daughters of Jerusalem now offer to seek along with Shulamith for her beloved, who had turned away and was gone. 1 Whither has thy beloved gone,    Thou fairest of women?    Whither has thy beloved turned,    That we may seek him with thee? <div eID="gen12643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12644" type="x-p"/> The longing remains with her even after she has wakened, as the after effect of her dream. In the morning she goes forth and meets with the daughters of Jerusalem. They cause Shulamith to describe her friend, and they ask whither he has gone. They wish to know the direction in which he disappeared from her, the way which he had probably taken (פנה, R. פן .R, to drive, to urge forward, to turn from one to another), that with her they might go to seek him (<hi type="italic">Vav</hi> of the consequence or the object, as at <reference osisRef="Ps.83.17">Psa 83:17</reference>). The answer she gives proceeds on a conclusion which she draws from the inclination of her beloved.
entries.33ea0fdfab1726287ec676593793a16ba0b87387: Sol 6:2 2 My beloved has gone down into the garden,    To the beds of sweet herbs,    To feed in the gardens    And gather lilies. <div eID="gen12644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12645" type="x-p"/> He is certainly, she means to say, there to be found where he delights most to tarry. He will have gone down - viz. from the palace (Sol 6:11; cf. 1Ki 20:43 and <reference osisRef="Esth.7.7">Est 7:7</reference>) - into his garden, to the fragrant beds, there to feed in his garden and gather lilies (cf. Old Germ. “to collect <hi type="italic">rôsen</hi>”); he is fond of gardens and flowers. Shulamith expresses this in her shepherd-dialect, as when Jesus says of His Father (Joh 15:1), “He is the husbandman.” Flowerbeds are the feeding place (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding לרעות under Sol 2:16) of her beloved. Solomon certainly took great delight in gardens and parks, Ecc 2:5. But this historical fact is here idealized; the natural flora which Solomon delighted in with intelligent interest presents itself as a figure of a higher Loveliness which was therein as it were typically manifest (cf. <reference osisRef="Rev.7.17">Rev 7:17</reference>, where the “Lamb,” “feeding,” and “fountains of water,” are applied as anagogics, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, heavenward-pointing types). Otherwise it is not to be comprehended why it is lilies that are named. Even if it were supposed to be implied that lilies were Solomon’s favourite flowers, we must assume that his taste was determined by something more than by form and colour. The words of Shulamith give us to understand that the inclination and the favourite resort of her friend corresponded to his nature, which is altogether thoughtfulness and depth of feeling (cf. under <reference osisRef="Ps.92.5">Psa 92:5</reference>, the reference to Dante: the beautiful women who gather flowers representing the paradisaical life); lilies, the emblems of unapproachable grandeur, purity inspiring reverence, high elevation above that which is common, bloom there wherever the lily-like one wanders, whom the lily of the valley calls her own. With the words:
entries.cf2054ec590333a3c9d5a9b92c6fe69c8410784f: Sol 6:3 3 I am my beloved’s, and my beloved is mine,    Who feeds among the lilies, <div eID="gen12645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12646" type="x-p"/> Shulamith farther proceeds, followed by the daughters of Jerusalem, to seek her friend lost through her own fault. She always says, not אישׁי, but דּודי and רעי; for love, although a passion common to mind and body, is in this Song of Songs viewed as much as possible apart from its basis in the animal nature. Also, that the description hovers between that of the clothed and the unclothed, gives to it an ideality favourable to the mystical interpretation. Nakedness is ערוה. But at the cross nakedness appears transported from the sphere of sense to that of the supersensuous.
entries.1eea67b25360e9defdc3bfdfc88666647dfd631f: Sol 6:4 <div eID="gen12646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12647" type="x-p"/> With Sol 6:4 Solomon’s address is resumed, and a new scene opens. Shulamith had found him again, and she who is beautiful in herself appears now so much the more beautiful, when the joy of seeing him again irradiates her whole being. 4 Beautiful art thou, my friend, as Tirzah,    Comely as Jerusalem,    Terrible as a battle-array. <div eID="gen12647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12648" type="x-p"/> In the praise of her beauty we hear the voice of the king. The cities which are the highest ornament of his kingdom serve him as the measure of her beauty, which is designated according to the root conceptions by יפה, after the equality of completeness; by נאוה, after the quality of that which is well-becoming, pleasing. It is concluded, from the prominence given to Tirzah, that the Song was not composed till after the division of the kingdom, and that its author was an inhabitant of the northern kingdom; for Tirzah was the first royal city of this kingdom till the time of Omri, the founder of Samaria. But since, at all events, it is Solomon who here speaks, so great an historical judgment ought surely to be ascribed to a later poet who has imagined himself in the exact position of Solomon, that he would not represent the king of the undivided Israel as speaking like a king of the separate kingdom of Israel. The prominence given to Tirzah has another reason. Tirzah was discovered by Robinson on his second journey, 1852, in which Van de Velde accompanied him, on a height in the mountain range to the north of Nablûs, under the name <hi type="italic">Tullûzah</hi>. Brocardus and Breydenback had already pointed out a village called <hi type="italic">Thersa</hi> to the east of Samaria. This form of the name corresponds to the Heb. better than that Arab. Tullûzah; but the place is suitable, and if <hi type="italic">Tullûzah</hi> lies high and beautiful in a region of olive trees, then it still justifies its ancient name, which means pleasantness or sweetness. But it cannot be sweetness on account of which Tirzah is named before Jerusalem, for in the eye of the Israelites Jerusalem was “the perfection of beauty” (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.2">Psa 50:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.2.15">Lam 2:15</reference>). That there is gradation from Tirzah to Jerusalem (Hengst.) cannot be said; for נאוה (<hi type="italic">decora</hi>) and יפה (<hi type="italic">pulchra</hi>) would be reversed if a climax were intended. The reason of it is rather this, that Shulamith is from the higher region, and is not a daughter of Jerusalem, and that therefore a beautiful city situated in the north toward Sunem must serve as a comparison of her beauty. That Shulamith is both beautiful and terrible (אימּה from אים) is not contradiction: she is terrible in the irresistible power of the impression of her personality, terrible as nîdgaloth, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, as troops going forth with their banners unfurled (cf. the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> of this <hi type="italic">v. denom</hi>., <reference osisRef="Ps.20.6">Psa 20:6</reference>). We do not need to supply מצנות, which is sometimes fem., <reference osisRef="Ps.25.3">Psa 25:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.32.9">Gen 32:9</reference>, although the attribute would here be appropriate, Num 2:3, cf. Song Num 10:5; still less צבאות, which occurs in the sense of military service, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.2">Isa 40:2</reference>, and a war-expedition, <reference osisRef="Dan.8.12">Dan 8:12</reference>, but not in the sense of war-host, as fem. Much rather nidgaloth, thus neut., is meant of bannered hosts, as ארחות (not אר), <reference osisRef="Isa.21.13">Isa 21:13</reference>, of those that are marching. War-hosts with their banners, their standards, go forth confident of victory. Such is Shulamith’s whole appearance, although she is unconscious of it - <hi type="italic">a veni, vidi, vici</hi>. Solomon is completely vanquished by her. But seeking to maintain himself in freedom over against her, he cries out to her:
entries.efc0b1e446e878448ec2ea4d985b832b35cc404e: Sol 6:5-7 5 <hi type="italic">a</hi> Turn away thine eyes from me,      For overpoweringly they assail me. <div eID="gen12648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12649" type="x-p"/> Döpke translates,<hi type="italic">ferocire me faciunt</hi>; Hengst.: they make me proud; but although הרהיב, after <reference osisRef="Ps.138.3">Psa 138:3</reference>, may be thus used, yet that would be an effect produced by the eyes, which certainly would suggest the very opposite of the request to turn them away. The verb רהב means to be impetuous, and to press impetuously against any one; the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. is the intens. of this trans. signification of the <hi type="italic">Kal</hi>: to press overpoweringly against one, to infuse terror, <hi type="italic">terrorem incutere</hi>. The lxx translates it by ἀναπτεροῦν, which is also used of the effect of terror (“to make to start up”), and the Syr. by afred, to put to flight, because arheb signifies to put in fear, as also arhab = khawwaf, <hi type="italic">terrefacere</hi>; but here the meaning of the verb corresponds more with the sense of Arab. r''b, to be placed in the state of ro'b, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, of paralyzing terror. If she directed her large, clear, penetrating eyes to him, he must sink his own: their glance is unbearable by him. This peculiar form the praise of her eyes here assume; but then the description proceeds as at <hi type="italic">Sol 4:1</hi>, <hi type="italic">Sol 2:3</hi>. The words used there in praise of her hair, her teeth, and her cheeks, are here repeated. 5 <hi type="italic">b</hi> Thy hair is like a flock of goats      Which repose downwards on Giliad. 6 Thy teeth like a flock of lambs    Which come up from the washing,    All of them bearing twins,    And a bereaved one is not among them. 7 Like a piece of pomegranate thy temples    Behind thy veil. <div eID="gen12649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12650" type="x-p"/> The repetition is literal, but yet not without change in the expression, - there, גל מהר, here, מן־הגּל; there, הקּץ, <hi type="italic">tonsarum</hi>, here, הרח, <hi type="italic">agnarum</hi> (Symm., Venet. τῶν ἀμναìδων); for רחל, in its proper signification, is like the Arab. rachil, richl, richleh, the female lamb, and particularly the ewe. Hitzig imagines that Solomon here repeats to Shulamith what he had said to another <hi type="italic">donna</hi> chosen for marriage, and that the flattery becomes insipid by repetition to Shulamith, as well as also to the reader. But the romance which he finds in the Song is not this itself, but his own palimpsest, in the style of Lucian’s transformed ass. The repetition has a morally better reason, and not one so subtle. Shulamith appears to Solomon yet more beautiful than on the day when she was brought to him as his bride. His love is still the same, unchanged; and this both she and the reader or hearer must conclude from these words of praise, repeated now as they were then. There is no one among the ladies of the court whom he prefers to her, - these must themselves acknowledge her superiority.
entries.db8d1bbc11e3e29019402d50cb8424592e0928ff: Sol 6:8-9 8 There are sixty queens,    And eighty concubines,    And virgins without number. 9 One is my dove, my perfect one, -    The only one of her mother,    The choice one of her that bare her.    The daughters saw her and called her blessed, -    Queens and concubines, and they extolled her. <div eID="gen12650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12651" type="x-p"/> Even here, where, if anywhere, notice of the difference of gender was to be expected, המּה stands instead of the more accurate הנּה (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Gen.6.2">Gen 6:2</reference>). The number off the women of Solomon’s court, 1Ki 11:3, is far greater (700 wives and 300 concubines); and those who deny the Solomonic authorship of the Song regard the poet, in this particular, as more historical than the historian. On our part, holding as we do the Solomonic authorship of the book, we conclude from these low numbers that the Song celebrates a love-relation of Solomon’s at the commencement of his reign: his luxury had not then reached the enormous height to which he, the same Solomon, looks back, and which he designates, <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.8">Ecc 2:8</reference>, as <hi type="italic">vanitas vanitatum</hi>. At any rate, the number of 60 מלכות, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, legitimate wives of equal rank with himself, is yet high enough; for, according to <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.21">2Ch 11:21</reference>, Rehoboam had 18 wives and 60 concubines. The 60 occurred before, at Sol 3:7. If it be a round number, as sometimes, although rarely, <hi type="italic">sexaginta</hi> is thus used (Hitzig), it may be reduced only to 51, but not further, especially here, where 80 stands along with it. פילגשׁ (פּלּגשׁ), Gr. παìλλαξ παλλακηì (Lat. <hi type="italic">pellex</hi>), which in the form פּלּקתּא (פּלקתא) came back from the Greek to the Aramaic, is a word as yet unexplained. According to the formation, it may be compared to חרמשׁ, from חרם, to cut off; whence also the harem bears the (Arab.) name hòaram, or the separated <hi type="italic">synaeconitis</hi>, to which access is denied. And ending in is (ש) is known to the Assyr., but only as an adverbial ending, which, as 'istinis = לבדּו, alone, solus, shows is connected with the pron. <hi type="italic">su</hi>. These two nouns appear as thus requiring to be referred to <hi type="italic">quadrilitera</hi>, with the annexed שׁ; perhaps פלגשׁ, in the sense of to break into splinters, from פּלג, to divide (whence a brook, as dividing itself in its channels, has the name of פּלג), points to the polygamous relation as a breaking up of the marriage of one; so that a concubine has the name pillěgěsh, as a representant of polygamy in contrast to monogamy. <div eID="gen12651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12652" type="x-p"/> In the first line of Sol 6:9 אחת is subj. (one, who is my dove, my perfect one); in the second line, on the contrary, it is pred. (one, <hi type="italic">unica</hi>, is she of her mother). That Shulamith was her mother’s only child does not, however, follow from this; אחת, <hi type="italic">unica</hi>, is equivalent to <hi type="italic">unice dilecta</hi>, as יחיד, <reference osisRef="Prov.4.3">Pro 4:3</reference>, is equivalent to <hi type="italic">unice dilectus</hi> (cf. Keil’s Zec 14:7). The parall. בּרה has its nearest signification <hi type="italic">electa</hi> (lxx, Syr., Jerome), not <hi type="italic">pura</hi> (Venet.); the fundamental idea of cutting and separating divides itself into the ideas of choosing and purifying. The Aorists, <hi type="italic">Sol 6:9</hi>, are the only ones in this book; they denote that Shulamith’s look had, on the part of the women, this immediate result, that they willingly assigned to her the good fortune of being preferred to them all, - that to her the prize was due. The words, as also at <reference osisRef="Prov.31.28">Pro 31:28</reference>, are an echo of <reference osisRef="Gen.30.13">Gen 30:13</reference>, - the books of the <hi type="italic">Chokma</hi> delight in references to Genesis, the book of pre-Israelitish origin. Here, in Sol 6:8, Sol 6:9, the distinction between our typical and the allegorical interpretation is correctly seen. The latter is bound to explain what the 60 and the 80 mean, and how the wives, concubines, and “virgins” of the harem are to be distinguished from each other; but what till now has been attempted in this matter has, by reason of its very absurdity or folly, become an easy subject of wanton mockery. But the typical interpretation regards the 60 and the 80, and the unreckoned number, as what their names denote, - viz. favourites, concubines, and serving-maids. But to see an allegory of heavenly things in such a herd of women - a kind of thing which the Book of Genesis dates from the degradation of marriage in the line of Cain - is a profanation of that which is holy. The fact is, that by a violation of the law of God (<reference osisRef="Deut.17.17">Deu 17:17</reference>), Solomon brings a cloud over the typical representation, which is not at all to be thought of in connection with the Antitype. Solomon, as Jul Sturm rightly remarks, is not to be considered by himself, but only in his relation to Shulamith. In Christ, on the contrary, is no imperfection; sin remains in the congregation. In the Song, the bride is purer than the bridegroom; but in the fulfilling of the Song this relation is reversed: the bridegroom is purer than the bride.
entries.4ab141b78ee6ad96dd127c6aeb23d286e67a2402: Sol 6:10 10 Who is this that looketh forth like the morning-red,      Beautiful as the moon, pure as the sun,      Terrible as a battle-host? <div eID="gen12652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12653" type="x-p"/> The question, “Who is this?” is the same as at Sol 3:6. There, it refers to her who was brought to the king; here, it refers to her who moves in that which is his as her own. There, the “this” is followed by עלה appositionally; here, by הנּשׁ looking forth determ., and thus more closely connected with it; but then indeterm., and thus apposit. predicates follow. The verb שׁקף signifies to bend forward, to overhang; whence the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. השׁקיף and <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. שׁקף, to look out, since in doing so one bends forward (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., under <reference osisRef="Ps.14.2">Psa 14:2</reference>). The lxx here translates it by ἐκκυìπτουσα, the Venet. by παρακυìπτουσα, both of which signify to look toward something with the head inclined forward. The point of comparison is, the rising up from the background: Shulamith breaks through the shades of the garden-grove like the morning-red, the morning dawn; or, also: she comes nearer and nearer, as the morning-red rises behind the mountains, and then fills always the more widely the whole horizon.
